newsitem.title: UK: UK watchdog may cast cloud over public finances.
newsitem.headline: UK watchdog may cast cloud over public finances.

text.p: An independent report on new government assumptions underlying Britain's public finances is likely to conclude the previous administration's forecasts for jobs and growth were too optimistic.

City analysts said the National Audit Office(NAO) report, due at 1430 GMT on Thursday, is also likely to back the Labour government if it rejects the practice of factoring in privatisation proceeds to budget calculations before legislation is drawn up.
The NAO, an independent watchdog, may also conclude that plans from the previous government to recoup billions of pounds in tax receipts are unrealistic.
"The report is likely to present a more gloomy medium-term outlook of the public finances than we saw in the budget last November," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

Shortly after taking office on May 2, new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown made changes to budgetary assumptions made by the last government and on May 20 asked the NAO to review his new assumptions.

The watchdog will address three new economic assumptions -- on GDP growth, inflation and unemployment -- and two conventions -- the use of assumed future privatisation proceeds in the public accounts, and the so-called "spend-to-save" scheme.
In its November budget, the previous government claimed it could recoup 6.68 billion pounds of tax revenue if it spent 796 million pounds over the next three years clamping down on tax evasion.
The NAO was told to report well before Brown presents his first budget on July 2, which has led to speculation that he will seek to use its findings to justify tax rises.
Analysts expect the Chancellor will have lowered growth forecasts.

The previous Conservative government upped its forecast for economic growth in the short and medium term. It projected GDP growth of 3.5 percent this fiscal year and 3.0 percent next, with growth of 2.5 percent each year from 1999 onwards.

Former Chancellor Kenneth Clarke also changed the practice of assuming unemployment will stay constant and factored into the accounts a continually falling jobless total instead, which implied lower public spending on benefits.

"Clarke assumed that unemployment was falling and would continue to fall. He was right, and in fact unemployment has fallen further than even he thought, but I think the NAO will probably suggest the government reverts back to assuming unchanged unemployment," said Loynes.
The choice of the National Audit Office to carry out the review was criticised by Clarke who said it was an inappropriate body to conduct the review and not geared up to do the job.

Some economists said the NAO's skill in assessing long term growth forecasts may be questionable, but its expertise is accounting means its views on the "spend-to-save" plan and treatment of privatisation proceeds within the budget will carry Analysts said it was likely the new government will say the savings under the scheme will be far less dramatic and the NAO agree.
"It's quite likely the NAO will say the previous government's projected savings were far too optimistic," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.
A similar scaling back of projections of privatisation proceeds is also expected.

There was some criticism at the time of the last budget that the previous government's calculations assumed privatisations would continue to reel in around a billion pounds a year for the foreseeable future.
That budget assumed receipts of 2.0 billion pounds this fiscal year, falling to 1.5 billion pounds in 1998/99, falling again to 1.0 billion pounds for each year thereafter.

Those projected receipts count as 'negative spending' in the accounts, effectively offsetting a portion of departmental spending. So they are crucial to the new government's expenditure plans, given its commitment to meet tight spending targets over the next two years.
Brown is likely to have revised down expected proceeds, or even recommended they are not included in the accounts until plans for further asset sell-offs are more advanced.
"The audit office may say this is more sensible -- to keep proceeds out of the picture at least until the legislation is drawn up," said Dicks. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
